verdict_reasoning: The goal is stated and the benchmarks are detailed, but the design of support procedure 7 is not settled. The int4 callback copies nbtree search rules (maintenance-fit-1), and the two documentation hunks describe different contracts (standards-compat-1). The thread does not measure the existing SortSupport comparator as an alternative (already-exists-1). Message #3 proposes a different split and has no answer, so the list has to agree on the callback contract before code review makes sense.

brief.title: Optional B-tree support procedure for specialized in-page searches
brief.problem: B-tree page searches call the comparison function through fmgr and deform each index tuple. For simple fixed-width types such as int4, this overhead costs much more than the comparison itself, and it slows both searches and random insertions.
brief.proposed_design: A new optional B-tree support procedure 7 lets an opclass install C callbacks that compare an insertion key with a page tuple and search a whole page interval. The callback may decline a search, and nbtree then uses the generic code. The first patch implements this for single-column, same-type int4 indexes, and the second adds an interpolation probe that falls back to binary search unless the adjacent tuple proves the exact boundary.
user_visible_surface: New optional B-tree support function number 7 (binsearchsupport), returning the address of a C-callable page search function.
New built-in function btint4binsearchsupport(internal), registered in the int4_ops opclass.
C API in nbtree.h for opclass callbacks that compare keys and search a page interval.
CREATE/ALTER OPERATOR FAMILY accept support function 7 for btree; opclasscmds.c and nbtvalidate.c change.
author_claims: One million int4 index-only lookups on dense keys ran 35% faster (2.245 s to 1.470 s); the author calls this a favorable case.
Specialization alone gains about 3% to 12% across all tested distributions; interpolation adds up to 34% for near-linear keys.
Interpolation costs about 2% for probes outside the indexed range; regular pgbench point lookups gain about 2.5% to 3%.
Duplicate lookups with 16 clients regressed by about 1.3%; the author is investigating.
Text and UUID showed no convincing gain, so the author leaves them out.
brief.thread_state: Only the author and Yao Feng replied. Yao Feng posted patches that move the search loop into nbtsearch.c on the SortSupport model and add int8 support; the author has not answered, and CFbot reports the patch needs a rebase.
unclear: The author has not said whether he accepts Yao Feng's split between nbtsearch.c and nbtcompare.c.
The material does not say how amcheck or index corruption interacts with callbacks that read keys directly.
The author promised to move the tuple extraction refactoring into the first patch and rerun tests; no new version is visible.
The material does not say whether third-party opclasses or extensions are expected to use support procedure 7, or how stable that C API is.
The cause of the 1.3% regression with 16 clients is not explained.

prior_attempts.title: Delaying/avoiding BTreeTupleGetNAtts() call within _bt_compare()
prior_attempts.reason: The visible messages do not show why. Andres Freund suggested loading ntupatts where the code loads it today and changing only the loop termination, because the delayed load and extra branches could add stalls. Peter Geoghegan agreed to rework the patch that way, and the thread has no later message before the November 2020 withdrawal.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P4 cut per-call overhead inside the generic _bt_compare(). This proposal skips _bt_compare() for int4 through an opclass callback that reads the key directly and may add an interpolation probe.

prior_attempts.title: _bt_binsrch* improvements - equal-prefix-skip binary search
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P15 changed the generic _bt_binsrch loop to skip equal prefixes. This proposal keeps the generic loop and adds an opt-in per-opclass search for single-column, same-type keys.

objections.title: Search control flow copied into per-opclass callbacks in nbtcompare.c
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch changes how nbtree handles posting lists, pivot tuples or heap TID tie-breaking in nbtsearch.c. The int4 callback, and the int8 one proposed in message #3, keeps the old rules, and no test fails. Users of specialized opclasses get wrong search bounds only on pages that hit the changed case.
objections.argument: The commit message of 0001 says the int4 callback itself preserves NULLs, descending order, pivot tuples, heap TID tie breakers and posting lists. Message #3 confirms that nbtcompare.c duplicates the binary search loop, slot probing, TID tie-breaking and posting list traversal. Each added type then copies nbtree search rules again. Message #3 proposes keeping the loop in nbtsearch.c, but the author has not replied and no new version exists.
objections.author_must_show: Will the next version keep all search control flow in nbtsearch.c, so that a type callback holds only value extraction, comparison and interpolation math?

critic.reasoning: The 0001 commit message says the int4 callback itself handles pivot tuples, heap TID tie breakers and posting lists. Message #3 confirms the duplicated loop, and no version that centralizes it in nbtsearch.c is visible.

objections.title: Support procedure 7 contract is not settled before it becomes permanent
objections.failure_scenario: An extension author follows xindex.sgml and writes a support function 7 that returns a whole-page search function. A later release adopts the primitive-callback split from message #3, and the extension opclass then fails to compile or gives wrong search results. The author finds out when users upgrade.
objections.argument: Support procedure numbers and their signatures become a documented, catalog-visible contract in pg_amproc and in CREATE OPERATOR CLASS. The docs disagree on what that contract is: xindex.sgml says the function returns the address of one search function, while btree.sgml says it installs callbacks. The name binsearchsupport names one algorithm, but patch 0002 adds interpolation. Message #3 proposes a different callback split on the model of sortsupport and skipsupport, and the author has not answered it.
objections.author_must_show: Which callback struct will support procedure 7 fill, does it follow the sortsupport and skipsupport pattern, and is it meant for third-party opclasses?

critic.reasoning: xindex.sgml says procedure 7 returns the address of one search function, while btree.sgml says it installs callbacks. Message #3 proposes a different callback split, and the thread has no answer to it, so the contract is not settled.

objections.title: Procedure 7 adds a second fast-comparator mechanism next to SortSupport
objections.failure_scenario: An opclass author who wants faster index searches for int8, date or timestamp must write new procedure 7 callbacks, even though the opclass already ships an fmgr-free comparator through support procedure 2. Each new type adds about 70 lines of search callbacks. A fix to ordering rules in one mechanism can be missed in the other.
objections.argument: btint4sortsupport and btint8sortsupport already give fmgr-free comparators that handle reverse order and NULL placement, so the specialization part of the win could come from calling the existing SortSupport comparator in _bt_compare, plus fast extraction of a fixed-width first key. Only the interpolation in the second patch needs type-specific knowledge. Message #3 shows the current split duplicates search control flow and needs new per-type code for int8, and it asks for the SortSupport model. The author has not answered message #3.
objections.author_must_show: What share of the 3-12% specialization gain remains if nbtree calls the existing SortSupport comparator, and what does procedure 7 add beyond the interpolation hook?

critic.reasoning: int4 and int8 already have fmgr-free comparators under support procedure 2, and the thread does not measure that route. The share of the 3% to 12% gain that needs a new procedure number is an open design question.

objections.title: Support procedure 7 exposes nbtree page internals as an extension API
objections.failure_scenario: An extension author implements support function 7 for a custom fixed-width type, following btree.sgml. A later release changes the index tuple or posting list layout. The extension's page search compiles and runs but reads keys wrongly, and users see wrong query results after upgrading.
objections.argument: The documentation offers support function 7 to any operator family, and its callbacks read keys directly and search a whole page. That makes the nbtree tuple layout part of a contract with code outside core. The material does not say whether third-party opclasses are expected to use it, or how stable the callback struct is. In [P6], Tom Lane rejected a change because it gave up page layout flexibility without a compelling gain, and the same cost applies here.
objections.author_must_show: Is support function 7 meant for third-party opclasses, and if so, which nbtree layout details does the callback API promise to keep stable?

precedents.title: Preventing indirection for IndexPageGetOpaque for known-size page special areas

critic.reasoning: btree.sgml offers procedure 7 to any operator family, and the material does not say which layout details the callbacks may rely on. [P6] concerned a fixed special-area offset inside core, so it should not be used as support here.

objections.title: End-to-end gain is small outside server-side microbenchmarks
objections.failure_scenario: The project adds support procedure 7, a new C callback API and a second page-search path in nbtree. Users who run ordinary OLTP queries see about 3% or nothing, and the 16-client duplicate case regresses. Future nbtree changes must keep both search paths correct for years.
objections.argument: The 35% to 47% figures come from loops of one million server-side lookups. Message #1 reports that standard pgbench -S showed no measurable difference, and message #2 reports about 2.5% to 3% for regular point lookups. The thread has no field report or production profile where in-page search dominates. The benefit reaches all int4 users, but its size in real workloads is not yet shown against the cost of a second search path.
objections.author_must_show: Which real workloads, such as nested loop joins, large IN lists or random inserts, gain end to end, with profiles showing page search as a real cost?

critic.reasoning: Message #2 does report a 6% to 10% insertion gain, and the server-side loop resembles a nested loop inner scan. Still, pgbench shows about 3%, one case regresses by 1.3% without explanation, and no profile from a real workload is shown.

Which callback struct does support procedure 7 fill, and does it return one search function (xindex.sgml) or install several callbacks (btree.sgml)?
What share of the 3% to 12% specialization gain remains if nbtree calls the existing SortSupport comparator and extracts the fixed-width key directly?

What causes the 1.3% regression for duplicate lookups with 16 clients, and which real workload shows a clear end-to-end gain with a profile?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows nbtree page search, posting lists and heap TID tie-breaking; none has spoken in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the correctness of a second nbtree search path and for a documented support procedure number and C callback API that stay for every later release.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted follow-up benchmarks in message #2 and promised a rework, but has not answered message #3, and the patch needs a rebase.

priority.reason: int4 B-tree indexes are common, and the specialization gain of 3% to 12% holds across the tested distributions. The callback contract and the split between nbtsearch.c and nbtcompare.c are still open, and a review of nbtree search correctness is costly.

provisional_note: Without the code, nobody can check that the interpolation probe stays inside the page's line pointer range on a corrupted page with unsorted keys. The cost of the new path for opclasses without support procedure 7 is also unchecked.

precedents_retrieved.title: enum support in btree_gin and btree_gist
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds enum support to the btree_gin and btree_gist extensions, without distance operators and so without KNN support. The enum comparison goes through enum_cmp_internal, which uses the type cache for enums whose values are not in OID order.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Testing showed that GiST comparisons gave wrong results after alter type ... add value, because enum_cmp_internal expects fcinfo->flinfo and DirectFunctionCallN passes NULL. The author agreed but had no time to do this before the end of the commitfest.

The problem is that the intermediate layer in btree_gist (and
probably btree_gin too, didn't look) does not pass through the
FunctionCallInfo data structure that's provided by the GIST AM.

A separate patch moves the negative infinity check for internal pages from _bt_compare() to _bt_binsrch().

precedents_retrieved.title: Use ReadRecentBuffer() for btree root page
precedents_retrieved.summary: Cache the btree root page's buffer ID per relation and use ReadRecentBuffer() in _bt_getroot() to skip the buffer mapping lookup. To make that scale, ReadRecentBuffer() would pin with PinBuffer() instead of taking the buffer header spinlock, which also bumps the usage count.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund objected to keeping the cached root buffer in rd_amcache, because each access method would then duplicate the same code. He suggested putting the fields in RelationData instead. Thomas Munro answered with an experimental LRU of recent lookups, and Andres said that should be a separate facility. No revised patch followed, so in January 2024 the entry was set to Waiting on Author, and the visible messages show no reply after that.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I am wondering if we don't want something more generic than stashing this in rd_amcache.

precedents_retrieved.title: Preventing indirection for IndexPageGetOpaque for known-size page special areas
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set adds a macro PageGetSpecialOpaque that finds an index page's opaque struct at a fixed offset from the page end, computed from BLCKSZ and the struct size, instead of reading pd_special. It also adds typed accessor macros for the btree and hash opaque areas, like those in GIN and GiST.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane, siding with Robert Haas, rejected the remaining fixed-offset part because it gives up page layout flexibility that may be needed later, for example for a per-page nonce. He also saw no hard evidence of a performance gain. Michael Paquier no longer wanted to switch from the page header to the opaque struct size, and Tom Lane rejected an alternative assertion-only check as redundant with _bt_checkpage.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It gives up page layout flexibility that
we might want back someday.  Moreover, I didn't see any hard evidence
offered that there's any actual performance gain, let alone such a
compelling gain that we should give up that flexibility for it.

precedents_retrieved.title: Floating point comparison inconsistencies of the geometric types
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patches remove the EPSILON-based fuzzy comparison macros (FPeq, FPlt, and others) from most geometric operators and use exact floating point comparison, with fuzzy comparison kept only for some lseg operators. They also rewrite some line operators to avoid division and add overflow, underflow and NaN checks, to allow default btree and hash operator classes and more index support later.
precedents_retrieved.objection: There was no agreement to remove the tolerance. Kyotaro HORIGUCHI argued that geometric types need a tolerance for floating point error, and Robert Haas rejected the GUC that came out of that discussion because indexes built under one setting could be invalid under another. Robert Haas noted that only the author clearly favoured removal and that nothing could be committed without agreement. The thread then went idle, the patches no longer applied, and David Steele returned the entry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Those problems boil down to "let's get rid of the tolerance
completely", and there's no consensus on that being a good thing to
do.

precedents_retrieved.title: Remove extra Sort node above a btree-compatible Index Scan
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes the planner's pathkey comparison so that an index from a B-tree-compatible access method in a different operator family is treated as matching the ORDER BY. This removes the extra Sort node above such an index scan, as seen with the xtree test module from the Index AM API cleanup series.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the patch ignores the operator family when deciding whether two pathkeys represent the same ordering, as in create_mergejoin_plan(). He said pathkeys are designed so that pointer comparison of canonical pathkeys is enough, and that the patch may cover up a break in that design. The author answered with context, and no revised patch appears in the visible messages.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
You can't just ignore the opfamily
etc. while deciding whether two pathkeys represent the same sort
ordering, as you did in create_mergejoin_plan().

precedents_retrieved.title: Eliminating CREATE INDEX comparator TID tie-breaker overhead
precedents_retrieved.summary: Replace the heap-TID tie-breaker in comparetup_index_btree() and comparetup_index_hash() for in-memory CREATE INDEX sorts with an ordinal number stored in SortTuple.tupindex, avoiding pointer chasing to the IndexTuple. This relies on the assumption that index tuplesort callers always feed heap tuples in physical (TID) order.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas objected that the optimization makes tuplesort.c depend on callers supplying tuples in TID order, which breaks it as an abstraction layer and burdens future work such as synchronized or parallel scans. He suggested instead establishing whether TID ordering of duplicates is actually valuable, and removing the tie-breaker only if it is not. No one else supported the patch, so there was no consensus, and the author withdrew it rather than continue the debate.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I'm not going to endorse the
notion that tuplesort.c will only DTRT if it receives tuples in TID
order; it cannot be the responsibility of the caller of the sort code
to ensure that the tuples are sorted.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
Reverted commit(s): Optimize order of GROUP BY keys
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit db0d67db2401eb6238ccc04c6407a4fd4f985832 and
several follow-on fixes.  The idea of making a cost-based choice
of the order of the sorting columns is not fundamentally unsound,
but it requires cost information and data statistics that we don't
really have.  For example, relying on procost to distinguish the
relative costs of different sort comparators is pretty pointless
so long as most such comparator functions are labeled with cost 1.0.
Moreover, estimating the number of comparisons done by Quicksort
requires more than just an estimate of the number of distinct values
in the input: you also need some idea of the sizes of the larger
groups, if you want an estimate that's good to better than a factor of
three or so.  That's data that's often unknown or not very reliable.
Worse, to arrive at estimates of the number of calls made to the
lower-order-column comparison functions, the code needs to make
estimates of the numbers of distinct values of multiple columns,
which are necessarily even less trustworthy than per-column stats.
Even if all the inputs are perfectly reliable, the cost algorithm
as-implemented cannot offer useful information about how to order
sorting columns beyond the point at which the average group size
is estimated to drop to 1.

Close inspection of the code added by db0d67db2 shows that there
are also multiple small bugs.  These could have been fixed, but
there's not much point if we don't trust the estimates to be
accurate in-principle.

Finally, the changes in cost_sort's behavior made for very large
changes (often a factor of 2 or so) in the cost estimates for all
sorting operations, not only those for multi-column GROUP BY.
That naturally changes plan choices in many situations, and there's
precious little evidence to show that the changes are for the better.
Given the above doubts about whether the new estimates are really
trustworthy, it's hard to summon much confidence that these changes
are better on the average.

Since we're hard up against the release deadline for v15, let's
revert these changes for now.  We can always try again later.

Note: in v15, I left T_PathKeyInfo in place in nodes.h even though
it's unreferenced.  Removing it would be an ABI break, and it seems
a bit late in the release cycle for that.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent records a rejection reason that applies here: P4 and P15 were withdrawn with no reason recorded. P6 concerns fixed special-area offsets, which this proposal does not change. Message #1 says the idea was first presented at PGConf.dev 2024, but the thread reports no discussion or objections from that talk.
There is no SQL syntax, GUC or default behaviour change, and built-in opclasses are not dumped, so pg_dump round-trip is not affected for most users. Unsupported searches fall back to procedure 1.

No objection from the replication and on-disk angle: the proposal changes no on-disk format, WAL record, wire protocol message or replicated state. It adds one pg_amproc row and one pg_proc entry, which initdb creates, and pg_upgrade needs no work because support procedure 7 is optional for user opclasses. Standbys read the same pages with the same results, and no VACUUM-time state is created, so the nbtree VACUUM bookkeeping rule does not apply. The new nbtree.h callback API is a major-release-only extension surface, not a backpatch or ABI break. Without the code, nobody can check whether the interpolation probe stays inside the page's line pointer range when a corrupted page has unsorted keys.

The proposal does not change who can do what. Support procedure 7 takes and returns internal, like support procedures 2 and 6, so only a superuser can create one. Adding it to an operator class already needs superuser. Each callback reads keys from pages that nbtree already reads. Robustness against corrupt pages, such as an interpolation probe computed from damaged first and last keys, is an amcheck and implementation question for another angle. It needs the code to check.

The nbtree VACUUM bookkeeping invariant does not apply, because the patch does not change VACUUM. Hot-path cost for non-users looks small from the prose, but the 1.3% regression with 16 clients is not explained. No nbtree committer has engaged in the visible thread, which is a committability concern only.
No contrib module or extension does in-page B-tree search specialization, because it needs nbtree internals. The only overlap from this angle is with SortSupport, raised above.
Demand for faster B-tree lookups on integer keys is broad, so this is a request to show real-workload gain, not a rejection.
